messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo energy harvester (sinusoidal current source, $C_p$ in parallel).
    *   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ via a storage capacitor at `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out, min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{out, max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (0.7-0.8s)
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (cold start to 1.8V)
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (change in mean 0.6-0.7s vs 0.7-0.8s)
    *   Piezo parameters: $I_p$ (30-100 $\mu$A), $f$ (80-100 Hz), $C_p$ (25-30 nF).
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$. For S1: $50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
    *   Load $R_L$: 150 k$\Omega$ (heavy) to 2200 k$\Omega$ (light).

    *   FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) failed:
        *   S2 (Heavy load): $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$ (FAIL - too low)
        *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): $V_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$ (FAIL - too high)
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$ (FAIL - too low)
        *   S5 (Low frequency): $dv$ FAIL (possibly not settled)
    *   The FBR is passive. It suffers from diode drops (~0.25-0.5V) and cannot regulate the output voltage.
    *   The $V_{oc}$ is quite low (approx 3.2V), meaning diode drops are significant.
    *   To improve $V_{avg}$ for S2/S4, we need better efficiency (synchronous rectification or SSHI).
    *   To prevent $V_{max}$ from exceeding 3.6V in S3, we need a clamp (Zener) or a regulator.

    *   *Option 1: Synchronous Switching Standard Converter (SSSC).*
        This uses switches to flip the voltage across $C_p$, effectively increasing the voltage transferred to the storage capacitor. However, it usually involves an inductor to invert the charge.
    *   *Option 2: Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE).*
        Similar goal, extracts charge at peaks.
    *   *Option 3: Improved FBR with Zener Clamp.*
        Adding a Zener diode (DZ33) will solve the $V_{max}$ problem for S3. However, the voltage drop in FBR still makes S2/S4 fail.
    *   *Option 4: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).*
        Using switches instead of diodes to reduce voltage drop.
    *   *Option 5: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).*
        A classic piezo harvester circuit. It uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, significantly increasing the available voltage.

    *   **Design A: SSHI-like (Inverter + Rectifier).**
        The standard SSHI uses a switch and inductor to flip $C_p$ voltage.
        Circuit:
        - Inductor $L_1$ and Switch $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo (or in a way that flips $V_{pzp}-V_{pzn}$).
        - Full bridge (or half bridge) to rectify the flipped energy into $C_{out}$.
        Actually, a simpler SSHI (Parallel-SSHI) flips the voltage across the piezo.
        Let's try a basic SSHI:
        1. Piezo: pzp, pzn.
        2. Inverter: $L_1$ from pzp to n1, $S_1$ from n1 to pzn. SYNC G1 closes $S_1$ at peaks.
        3. Rectifier: Diodes from pzp to out, pzn to out (with ground returns). Or just a bridge.
        Wait, the "inverted" voltage is across the piezo. The rectification still happens.
        *Wait*, a simpler version is to use a synchronous bridge or just a bridge with an inductor-based voltage boost.

    *   **Design B: Active Rectifier (Synchronous Bridge).**
        Replace the diodes in the FBR with switches.
        - $S_1$: pzp to out
        - $S_2$: pzn to out
        - $S_3$: 0 to pzp
        - $S_4$: 0 to pzn
        - $G_1$: ctrl $S_1$ and $S_4$ (positive peak)
        - $G_2$: ctrl $S_2$ and $S_3$ (negative peak)
        This eliminates diode drops, helping S2/S4.

    *   **Design C: FBR + Zener Clamp + Boost/SSHI.**
        Let's combine the FBR with a Zener clamp (DZ33) to fix S3, and an inductor-switch flip (SSHI) to boost the voltage for S2/S4.

    *   A "Parallel SSHI" flips the voltage of the piezo at the extrema.
    *   $C_p$ is the piezo capacitance.
    *   At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, a switch closes $L$ in parallel with $C_p$ for $t_{on} = \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$, flipping the voltage to negative.
    *   This effectively increases the average voltage delivered to the rectifier.
    *   Structure:
        - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
        - Inverter: $L_1$ from pzp to n1, $S_1$ from n1 to pzn (S1 controlled by G1).
        - Rectifier: DSCH bridge (pzp -> out, pzn -> out, 0 -> pzp, 0 -> pzn).
        - Clamp: DZ33 from 0 to out.
        - Storage: $C_{out}$ from out to 0.

    *Wait*, the "inverter" should be in parallel with the piezo to flip its voltage.
    - $L_1$ from pzp to n1.
    - $S_1$ from n1 to pzn.
    - $G_1$ closes $S_1$ at peaks.
    - But the rectifier is also connected to pzp/pzn.
    - If we flip the voltage, the rectifier will still catch the peaks.

    *Refining the Active Bridge:*
    - SYNC controllers are limited to 2.
    - $G_1$: `edges: "both"`, `phase: 0`. Closes $S_1$ (pzp to out) and $S_2$ (0 to pzn) maybe? No, that's not right.
    - For a full bridge:
        - Pos half cycle: $pzp \to out$, $0 \to pzn$.
        - Neg half cycle: $pzn \to out$, $0 \to pzp$.
    - $G_1$ (pos edge): closes $S_{pzp-out}$ and $S_{0-pzn}$.
    - $G_2$ (neg edge): closes $S_{pzn-out}$ and $S_{0-pzp}$.
    - This uses 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.

    *Refining SSHI:*
    - Use 1 SYNC to flip the piezo voltage.
    - Use a standard FBR to rectify.
    - This uses 4 diodes, 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC.
    - Total components: 4D + 1L + 1S + 1G + 1C = 8.
    - This is very efficient and handles the low-voltage cases (S2, S4).
    - Add Zener clamp (DZ33) to handle S3. Total: 9.

    *Wait*, does the SSHI flip the voltage *before* the rectifier?
    Yes. $V_{pzp}$ reaches $V_{peak}$, then $S_1$ closes $L$ across it, flipping $V_{pzp}$ to $-V_{peak}$. The rectifier then sees a jump from $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$, effectively doubling the voltage swing and improving extraction.

    Let's try a Synchronous Bridge (Design B) and an SSHI+FBR+Zener (Design A).

    - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
    - Rectifier:
        - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
        - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    - Flip-circuit:
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn
        - G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=pi*sqrt(L*Cp)
    - Protection:
        - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    - Storage:
        - C1: out -> 0

    - S1: pzp -> out (ctrl G1)
    - S2: 0 -> pzn (ctrl G1)
    - S3: pzn -> out (ctrl G2)
    - S4: 0 -> pzp (ctrl G2)
    - G1: SYNC, edges="pos", phase=0
    - G2: SYNC, edges="neg", phase=0
    - C1: out -> 0
    - D1: 0 -> out (DZ33)

    *Self-Correction on Design B:*
    The SYNC controllers close switches for a very short `ton` (max 1ms). They are not meant to hold the switch closed for the entire half-period. They are designed for "charge extraction" or "voltage flipping".
    For an active bridge, the switches must be closed for the *entire* half-period.
    The SYNC description says: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    This means SYNC is **NOT** suitable for a continuous active bridge. It is designed for **SSH (Synchronized Switch Harvesting)**.

    Okay, so Design B is out. Design A (SSHI) is the way to go.

    Wait, is there a better way to use SYNC?
    The SYNC can be used for "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE).
    In SECE:
    - Piezo $C_p$ charges an inductor $L$ during the half-cycle.
    - At the peak, the switch $S_1$ closes, transferring the energy from $L$ (and $C_p$) to $C_{out}$.
    - Structure:
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> out
        - G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=small
        - C1: out -> 0
        - D1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        - (Need a way to handle the negative half cycle too).

    Let's stick to the SSHI + FBR approach. It's a well-known robust topology.

    *Wait, let's look at the FBR results again.*
    FBR fails S2 (heavy load, $V_{avg}=1.76\text{V}$) and S4 (weak excitation, $V_{avg}=1.51\text{V}$).
    The main problem is the diode drop. $V_{oc}$ is only 3.2V. Two diode drops (even Schottky) take away 0.5-0.7V.
    $3.2\text{V} - 0.5\text{V} = 2.7\text{V}$.
    But the load is drawing current, and the $V_{oc}$ is a peak value. The average voltage is lower.
    SSHI boosts the voltage by flipping the $C_p$ voltage, which effectively increases the voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *Actually*, there's a simpler SSHI called "Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo.
    - $S_1$: pzp -> n1, $L_1$: n1 -> pzn (or $L_1$ in series with $S_1$).
    - When $S_1$ closes, the energy in $C_p$ is transferred to $L_1$ and back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity.
    - This flips $V_{pzp}$ from $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$.

    Wait, the "FBR" (Full Bridge Rectifier) already uses 4 diodes. If I add the SSHI flip circuit, I have:
    4 Diodes + 1 Inductor + 1 Switch + 1 SYNC = 7 components.
    Add Zener clamp (DZ33) and Storage Cap = 9 components.
    Total $\le 16$. This is perfect.

    - Piezo: pzp, pzn
    - FBR:
        - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
        - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    - SSHI Inverter:
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn
        - G1: SYNC, edges="both", phase=0, ton=3e-05 (will be tuned)
    - Protection:
        - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    - Storage:
        - C1: out -> 0, value=2.2uF (will be tuned)

    *Check:*
    - S1: Nominal. Should be fine.
    - S2: Heavy load. SSHI boosts efficiency, should raise $V_{avg} > 1.8\text{V}$.
    - S3: Strong excitation. Zener clamp D5 keeps $V_{max} \le 3.3\text{V} + \text{small} \approx 3.4\text{V}$.
    - S4: Weak excitation. SSHI boosts efficiency, should raise $V_{avg} > 1.8\text{V}$.
    - S5: Low frequency. SSHI should still work.
    - S6: Hot/Cp+. SSHI should still work.

    Is there any other topology?
    Maybe a "Half-Bridge" if we can use a flying capacitor, but a full bridge is simpler.
    What about a "charge pump" style? Piezo is essentially a capacitor. We can use the SYNC to switch the piezo capacitor in series with the storage capacitor.

    Let's try the SSHI+FBR as the primary proposal.

    *Wait*, one detail: The "FBR" in the reference design failed S3 $V_{max}$ (5.72V). Adding the Zener clamp is essential.
    The reference design FBR had a storage cap of 2.2uF. I'll start with that.
    The `ton` for SSHI is typically $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
    If $L = 10\text{mH}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $ton = \pi\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi\sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    This is within the $1\mu\text{s}$ to $1\text{ms}$ range (Wait, the prompt says `1e-07..0.001`, so $0.1\mu\text{s}$ to $1\text{ms}$. Yes, it fits).

    Let's double check the component count:
    D1, D2, D3, D4, D5 (5 diodes)
    L1 (1 inductor)
    S1 (1 switch)
    G1 (1 SYNC)
    C1 (1 capacitor)
    Total = 9. (Limit is 16).

    Another idea: Instead of a full bridge, can we use a simpler rectifier?
    A half-bridge requires a capacitor at pzn.
    The full bridge is more robust.

    What about a Synchronous Rectifier using the SYNC?
    Wait, the SYNC only closes for `ton` seconds. It cannot be used for the whole half-cycle.
    So any "synchronous" part must be a pulse, like in SSHI or SECE.

    Wait, the prompt says: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    This is *exactly* what you need for SSHI. The flip occurs at the extrema.

    Let's refine the SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    Components:
    - D1: pzp -> out, DSCH
    - D2: pzn -> out, DSCH
    - D3: 0 -> pzp, DSCH
    - D4: 0 -> pzn, DSCH
    - D5: 0 -> out, DZ33
    - C1: out -> 0, 2.2uF
    - L1: pzp -> n1, 10mH
    - S1: n1 -> pzn, ctrl G1
    - G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=5e-05, phase=0

    One more check on the nodes for the bridge:
    - D1: ["pzp", "out"]
    - D2: ["pzn", "out"]
    - D3: ["0", "pzp"]
    - D4: ["0", "pzn"]
    This is a standard full-bridge rectifier.

    Wait, if $S_1$ and $L_1$ are in parallel with the piezo, the bridge is also in parallel.
    Is there any risk?
    When $S_1$ closes, the current will flow through the $L-S$ loop.
    The diodes will be reverse-biased or forward-biased depending on the voltage.
    At the positive peak, $V_{pzp}$ is max, $V_{pzn}$ is min.
    D1 is forward-biased (pzp -> out), D4 is forward-biased (0 -> pzn).
    Wait, when the switch closes, the current should ideally stay in the $L-C_p$ loop.
    The diode drops are small, but the energy is mostly in $C_p$.
    This is the standard SSHI configuration.

    Let's try this.

    *Alternative:* SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).
    In SECE, you have an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$.
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> out
    - G1: SYNC, edges="both"
    - This only works for the positive half-cycle. To do both, you need another L-S pair for the negative half-cycle.
    - L2: pzn -> n2, S2: n2 -> out.
    - This would be: L1, S1, L2, S2, G1, G2, C1, D5. (8 components).
    - SECE is often more efficient than SSHI because it's less dependent on the rectifier's diode drops (it bypasses them).
    - In SECE, at the peak, the switch closes and the charge is dumped from the inductor into $C_{out}$.
    - Let's try SECE as a second proposal.

    *SECE Structure:*
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> out, ctrl G1
    - L2: pzn -> n2
    - S2: n2 -> out, ctrl G2
    - G1: SYNC, edges="pos", phase=0
    - G2: SYNC, edges="neg", phase=0
    - C1: out -> 0
    - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)

    Wait, let's check SECE logic:
    In the positive half-cycle, $C_p$ charges $L_1$ through the piezo current source. At the peak, $S_1$ closes, and $L_1$ discharges into $C_{out}$.
    Wait, is $L_1$ connected to $pzp$ during the whole cycle?
    Yes. $L_1$ is between $pzp$ and $n1$, and $S_1$ is between $n1$ and $out$.
    During the half-cycle, the current $I_p$ flows through $L_1$ and $C_p$.
    $I_L = I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    The energy stored in the inductor is $1/2 L I_{peak}^2$.
    At the peak, the switch $S_1$ closes, and the energy is transferred to $C_{out}$.
    This is a very efficient way to harvest.

    Let's compare SSHI and SECE.
    SSHI: $L$ is in parallel with $C_p$, flips voltage. $C_p$ still provides energy to the rectifier.
    SECE: $L$ is in series with $C_p$, transfers energy at the peak.
    Both are good. Let's provide both and see.

    Wait, the "FBR" failed because of the diode drop. SECE has no diodes in the main power path (only the Zener clamp). This might be better for S2/S4.

    *Wait*, let's re-read the "FBR" reference.
    S4 (weak excitation, Ip=30uA): $V_{avg}=1.51\text{V}$.
    Load $R_L = 1000\text{k}\Omega$.
    Power $P = V^2/R_L = 1.51^2 / 1000\text{k} = 2.28\mu\text{W}$.
    The reference FBR barely missed $1.8\text{V}$. SECE should easily push it over $1.8\text{V}$ by removing the diode drops.

    Let's refine the SECE proposal:
    - L1: pzp -> n1, value=10mH
    - S1: n1 -> out, ctrl G1
    - L2: pzn -> n2, value=10mH
    - S2: n2 -> out, ctrl G2
    - G1: SYNC, edges="pos", ton=1e-04, phase=0
    - G2: SYNC, edges="neg", ton=1e-04, phase=0
    - C1: out -> 0, 2.2uF
    - D5: 0 -> out, DZ33

    *Self-Correction on SECE:*
    Actually, SECE usually requires the inductor to be in series with the piezo.
